ranges.en: Mishna lists women in sota-related cases, such as a confession, testimony of defilement, refusal to drink, or a husband who relents.
Mishna: meal-offerings of women married to priests are burned, but a priest's daughter married to an Israelite has her meal-offering eaten.
Mishna contrasts priests and priests' daughters: whose meal-offerings are eaten, and who is disqualified by forbidden intercourse.
Mishna continues: priests and priests' daughters differ in impurity from corpses and in eating offerings of the most sacred order.
Mishna lists differences between men and women: leprosy rites, vowing a son a nazirite, and shaving at the end of naziriteship.
Mishna lists differences between men and women in betrothing or selling a minor daughter, and in the forms of capital punishment.
Baraita: meal-offerings of women married into the priesthood are burned, but a handful is still removed and offered separately.
Asks whether the prohibition against burning part of an offering as fuel should apply to the remainder here.
Yehuda son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi: the remainder is burned as firewood, not as an offering, following Rabbi Eliezer.
Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer permits burning parts that may not be offered for a pleasing aroma, but only as firewood.
Asks: this works for Rabbi Eliezer, but what can the Rabbis who reject his reasoning say about burning the remainder?
Answer: the Rabbis follow the position of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon on how the remainder is handled.
Baraita: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon says the handful is offered alone and the remainder is scattered on the ash heap.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Clarifies that the Rabbis dispute Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon only over a sinner priest's meal-offering, and agree that a sota's remainder is scattered.
Asks the reason for the mishna's distinction between an Israelite woman married to a priest and a priest's daughter married to an Israelite.
Leviticus verse: a priest's meal-offering is wholly burned and not eaten, read as applying to priests but not to their daughters.
Mishna: a priest's daughter can be disqualified by forbidden intercourse, but a priest is not desacralized by it.
Asks from where this rule is derived.
Leviticus verse: the offspring are desacralized but the priest himself is not, read as the source of the rule.
Mishna: a priest's daughter may become impure through a corpse, but a priest may not.
Asks the reason for the difference in corpse impurity.
Leviticus verses: the command is addressed to the sons of Aaron, not their daughters, and only males may eat the most sacred meal-offering.
Mishna opens a list of halakhic differences between men and women.
Baraita derives from Leviticus that a leprous man's rending of clothes and growing of hair applies to men, not women.
Mishna: a man may vow his minor son a nazirite, but a woman may not vow her son a nazirite.
Rabbi Yochanan: the rule about vowing a son a nazirite is a halakha transmitted orally from Sinai.
Mishna: a man may shave using offerings from his father's naziriteship, but a woman may not use her father's offerings.
Rabbi Yochanan again: the nazirite rule is a Sinai tradition, not derived from Scripture.
Mishna: a man may betroth his minor daughter, but a woman may not betroth her daughter.
Deuteronomy verse: the father says I gave my daughter to this man, showing that only the father may betroth.
Mishna: a man may sell his daughter as a maidservant, but a woman may not sell her daughter.
Exodus verse: if a man sells his daughter as a maidservant, showing that only a man may sell her.
Mishna: a man is stoned naked, but a woman is not stoned naked.
Asks the reason for this rule, and what the word him in the verse excludes.
Objects: if him excludes her entirely, a contrary verse says to bring out that man or that woman and stone them.
Answer: him excludes his garment, so only a man is stoned without clothing, and a woman is not stoned without hers.
Mishna: a man is hanged after execution, but a woman is not hanged.
Asks the reason for the hanging rule.
Deuteronomy verse: you shall hang him, the man, and not her, the woman.
Mishna: a man is sold for his theft, but a woman is not sold for her theft.
Asks the reason for the theft-sale rule.
Exodus verse: he shall be sold for his theft, and not she for hers.
Chapter-closing formula, marking the end of this chapter and the start of the next.
Mishna: a betrothed woman and a widow awaiting a yavam who secluded herself after warning neither drink the water nor collect her ketuba.
Numbers verse: the sota is a wife under her husband, which excludes betrothed women and widows awaiting a yavam.
Mishna continues with women whose marriages were prohibited from the start, such as a widow of a High Priest or a mamzeret.

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a Gibeonite woman married to an Israelite, or an Israelite woman married to a mamzer or Gibeonite, neither drinks nor collects her ketuba.
Mishna introduces a further list of women who neither drink nor collect their ketuba.
Mishna: a woman who confesses she is defiled, or against whom witnesses testify, neither drinks nor collects her ketuba.
Mishna: a woman whose husband refuses to let her drink, or who was intimate with him on the way, collects her ketuba but does not drink.
Beit Shammai: if a sota's husband dies before she drinks, she collects her ketuba and does not drink.
Beit Hillel: in that case she either drinks or does not collect her ketuba.
Mishna: a woman pregnant or nursing by another man at her marriage neither drinks nor collects, according to Rabbi Meir.
The Rabbis: her husband may separate from her and remarry her after twenty-four months, so the marriage is permitted and she drinks.
Mishna: a barren woman, an elderly woman, or one unable to bear children neither collects her ketuba nor drinks.
Rabbi Elazar: a husband may marry another wife to have children, so these women are permitted; all other women drink or forfeit the ketuba.
Mishna: a priest's wife drinks and is permitted, as is a eunuch's wife; a warning covers all forbidden relatives except a minor.
Mishna: the court warns the wife of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or an imprisoned husband only to disqualify her from her ketuba, not to make her drink.
Rabbi Yosei: the court's warning also makes her drink, and when her husband is released he has her drink.
Asks what drinking means here, since she does not drink, and how the warning confers a status on her.
Baraita: the extra phrase and say unto them includes betrothed women and widows awaiting a yavam in the warning rule.
Asks whose opinion the mishna expresses.
The mishna expresses the opinion of Rabbi Yonatan.
Baraita on the verses: under your husband excludes a betrothed woman, and any man includes a widow awaiting a yavam, per Rabbi Yoshiya.
Rabbi Yonatan reads under your husband as excluding a widow awaiting a yavam, and the law of jealousy verse as excluding betrothed women.
Explains the dispute: Rabbi Yonatan sees the bond with a betrothed woman as stronger, since she is stoned for adultery, unlike the yavam's widow.
Rabbi Yoshiya sees the bond with the yavam's widow as stronger, since her marriage is completed by intercourse alone, so only betrothed women are excluded.
Asks what Rabbi Yonatan does with the phrase any man if he excludes both betrothed women and widows awaiting a yavam.
Answer: it includes the wives of a deaf-mute, of an imbecile, and others who remain under their husbands' authority.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what Rabbi Yoshiya does with the phrase under her husband, since he needs it for another purpose.
Rabbi Yoshiya uses the phrase to compare man to woman and woman to man, as explained later.
Asks why these verses are needed, since otherwise a betrothed woman would seemingly drink the water.
Rabbi Aha bar Chanina's baraita: the sota law applies only when the husband's intercourse preceded the paramour's, which excludes a betrothed woman.
Rami bar Chama: the extra exclusion is needed for a betrothed woman who had intercourse with her husband in her father's house before the adultery.
Objects: the parallel case of a yavam makes her a full wife, since Rav held that a yavam's intercourse makes her fully his wife.
Shmuel: a yavam acquires his yevama only for the matters stated in the levirate passage, so Rabbi Yonatan's view is consistent with him.
Asks whether Rav should instead be read as following Rabbi Yoshiya, and Shmuel as following Rabbi Yonatan.
Rav replies that he holds this even according to Rabbi Yonatan, since the verse needed to exclude such a yevama, implying she is a full wife otherwise.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel says he holds his view even by Rabbi Yoshiya, since the verse's specific inclusion implies she is not fully his wife.
Is forewarning required before a woman who already violates modesty loses her marriage contract payment, or is it unnecessary?
A mishna on betrothed women and yevamot not drinking, yet still losing payment, suggests warning is what causes the forfeit.
Abaye: the warning is meant to make her forbidden to the husband, not to forfeit her payment.
Rav Pappa: the warning is meant to make her drink, which applies when she is married and not when betrothed.
A baraita distinguishes betrothed from married women regarding warning them so that they drink the water.
Rava brings a mishna listing women who neither drink nor collect payment, as support for his reading.
If warning only forbids them, they are already forbidden; so the warning must be about forfeiting payment.
Rav Yehuda of Diskarta: the warning makes her forbidden to her paramour, as she is forbidden to her husband.
Rav Ḥanina of Sura introduces a proof from the mishna on women whom the court warns.
The court warns those whose husbands are incapacitated, not to make them drink but to disqualify their payment.
Conclusion: the mishna shows that a warning is required.
Why did the other Sages not derive the warning requirement from this explicit statement?
Perhaps those cases differ, since such a wife has no fear of her husband, so she must be warned.
If a woman violates the law and the husband wants to keep her, does the Torah's objection count as his objection?
The mishna on court warnings: if the husband could keep her, the court would act against a possibly unwanted warning.
Normally a husband wants to divorce a woman violating the law, so the court acts on that assumption.
If a husband warned his wife and then retracted, can he still retract, or is the warning now fixed?
The mishna shows the court warns; if the husband may retract, the court would act on a warning he can withdraw.
Normally a person agrees with the court and does not retract its warning, so the concern does not arise.
A mishna says the court gives two scholars to escort the sota; if he could retract, he would simply retract and have relations.
What is different about Torah scholars that they are chosen to escort the husband?
They can tell the husband to retract his warning and then lawfully have relations with her.
Rabbi Yoshiya's three rulings, reported by Ze'eira, include that a husband who retracted his warning has it retracted.
Ze'eira's report on the rulings is recounted, and the conclusion is that a husband can retract his warning.
Rav Aha and Ravina dispute whether retraction after seclusion is valid, and the Gemara adopts the view that it is not.
From where can one derive that retraction after seclusion is invalid?
A baraita of Rabbi Yosei: the husband of a sota is trusted, a fortiori from a menstruating woman's husband.
The Rabbis object: trust in the menstruating case is due to her ability to become permitted, which a sota lacks.
If retraction after seclusion were valid, the sota could become permitted; so the Rabbis' ruling shows it is not.
The mishna: if husbands die before the wives drink, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree about payment and drinking.
What is the basis of the disagreement between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel?
Beit Shammai hold that a promissory note to be collected is like one already collected, so payment is already in her possession.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Beit Hillel's view that an unpaid promissory note is not like paid, and the mishna on a pregnant woman, are restated.
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabba bar Avuh, limits the dispute between the tanna and Rabbi Elazar to barren and elderly women.
A sexually underdeveloped woman is excluded from the sota ritual by the verse requiring one whose way is to bear seed.
A baraita on a betrothed or yevama secluded before consummation seems to contradict Rav Naḥman's limit.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita: women pregnant or nursing by another man at marriage lose the sota ritual and payment, per Rabbi Meir, whose reasoning and Sages' ruling are given.
A young man who married a barren or elderly woman without prior children: the Rabbis deny her the ritual, while Rabbi Elazar permits it.
Further baraita cases: a warned or secluded betrothed woman, and wives of mamzerim, converts and sexually underdeveloped women, whose marriages are permitted.
The baraita's permitted-marriage ruling for a sexually underdeveloped woman is presented as refuting Rav Naḥman.
Rav Naḥman replies that this is a tanna dispute, and he follows the baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who excludes her.
What do the Rabbis do with the verse about seed, if they permit a sexually underdeveloped woman to drink?
The verse teaches that a barren woman will be remembered and conceive, as Rabbi Akiva holds.
Rabbi Yishmael objects that barren women would then seclude themselves, and the virtuous one would lose the blessing.
If so, what is the purpose of the verse about conceiving seed?
The verse means that future births will be easier and of better quality, such as males, taller and white children.
The Tosefta states that the wife of a mamzer in a permitted marriage drinks the water.
Is it not obvious that such a permitted marriage brings the ritual, and why would it be doubted?
It is taught so that one would not think she should not drink, lest mamzerim proliferate, which is not a concern.
Is it not obvious that converts and emancipated slaves in permitted marriages drink, and why would the verse exclude them?
The phrase speak to the children of Israel is an amplification that includes converts, so they do drink.
The mishna: the wife of a priest drinks the water and, if found innocent, is permitted to her husband.
Why state it, since she might be thought exempt because a raped priest's wife is forbidden to him?
The verse distinguishes seized and unseized women, and the mishna teaches that the priest's wife still drinks.
Is it not obvious that the priest's wife is permitted after being found innocent?
Rav Huna explains the mishna as referring to a woman whose health deteriorates after drinking, though not as a sota.
Once the water has tested her, why would deteriorating health suggest she is defiled, since the case might be licentious?
Her deteriorating health indicates nothing, since even rape by another man would make a priest's wife forbidden.
The mishna: the wife of a eunuch drinks the water.
Is it not obvious that a eunuch's wife, in a permitted marriage, drinks the water?
The verse says if another man lay with her besides her husband, teaching that a eunuch's wife still drinks.
Is it not obvious that a husband may warn his wife regarding all forbidden relations, such as with her father or brother?

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Might one think the sota ritual does not apply to a woman secluded with a forbidden relative, since she is already forbidden?
The double phrase she was defiled teaches that warning applies even for forbidden relatives, so the ritual still applies.
The mishna: a husband may warn his wife about all forbidden men, except a minor and one who is not a man.
What does the phrase not a man exclude?
If it excludes a shaḥuf, that conflicts with Shmuel's view that a shaḥuf can disqualify a priest's daughter from teruma.

Baraita: wherever ko, kakha, or speaking and saying appears, it refers to Hebrew, citing Numbers 6:23 and Deuteronomy 25:9.
Asks how the blessings and curses were carried out.
Mishna cited: how the ceremony took place once Israel crossed the Jordan.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda explains the locations in Deuteronomy 11:30, placing Gerizim and Ebal near Shechem by the oaks of Moreh.
Genesis 12:6 is cited: the oaks of Moreh there are at Shechem, so the same identification applies here.
Baraita: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei says he refuted the Samaritans, who identify Shechem but reject verbal analogies.
Rabbi Elazar explains beyond the Jordan as meaning near it, since the Jordan was the crossing point.
Deuteronomy 27:4 is cited: setting up stones on Ebal after crossing the Jordan implies Ebal is near the crossing.
Rabbi Elazar reads the verse as the west, Canaanite land, and mountains near Gilgal, and holds Gerizim and Ebal are closer to the Jordan.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds the verse teaches the route for entering Canaan, the way, settled areas, and plains.
Tosefta: the Ark led the crossing of the Jordan on that day, carried by the priests rather than the Levites, citing Joshua 3:11 and 3:13.
Rabbi Yosei: the priests carried the Ark in three places, at the Jordan crossing, around Jericho, and when it returned to the Holy of Holies.

34a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Once the priests' feet touched the Jordan, the water flowed back, as stated in the Torah's account of the crossing.
Joshua 3:15 is cited: the carriers reached the Jordan and the waters from above stood still in one heap.
Rabbi Yehuda holds the water rose twelve mil high, opposite the camp of Israel.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon objects: water moves faster than people, so twelve-mil water would have drowned the camp before crossing.
Replies that the water piled in heaps over three hundred mil high, until all the kings of East and West saw it, citing Joshua 5:1.
Rahab's words and the Israelite spies' report, Joshua 2:10 and 2:11, show the Canaanites were terrified by the Red Sea miracle.
While still in the Jordan, Joshua told them their purpose is to drive out the inhabitants, and that if not, the water would drown them.
Asks what the word otikhem in Joshua's warning means.
Otikhem is a combination of the word for me and the word for you, so it means me and you.
While still in the Jordan, Joshua ordered each man to lift a stone on his shoulder, one for each tribe.
Joshua 4:6 is cited: the stones are a sign for children asking what they mean, that their fathers crossed the Jordan.
Joshua instructed them to take twelve stones from the Jordan, carry them over, and lay them down in the lodging place that night.
Explains that where you lodge this night means only that night, not at every lodging place.
Rabbi Yehuda reports the stones weighed about forty se'a each, and a load one lifts is a third of what one can carry.
The spies' cluster in Numbers 13:23 is used to calculate its weight of 480 se'a, since it was carried on two poles by four people.
Rabbi Yitzhak explains the spies' carrying arrangement: eight carried the cluster, one a pomegranate, one a fig, and Joshua and Caleb carried nothing.
Gives two reasons Joshua and Caleb carried nothing: their dignity, or that they did not share in the spies' wicked counsel.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha dispute the tannaitic height of the water; one holds it follows Rabbi Yehuda's twelve mil.

34b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon holds the people crossed in the same formation they camped, one after another, with water standing very high.
Other Sages hold that all agree on the formation, but disagree whether a person or water moves faster.
Explains that the command send you was given at Moses' discretion, since God would not choose a bad portion for them.
Deuteronomy 1:23 is cited: it was good in my eyes, which Reish Lakish reads as good in Moses' eyes but not God's.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba holds the spies intended only to shame the land of Israel.
Numbers 13 and Isaiah 24:23 are compared using the same verb for search and shame, supporting Rabbi Hiyya's reading.
Rabbi Yitzhak transmits that the spies were named for their deeds, explaining Sethur and Michael as hiding and weakening God's acts.
Rabbi Yohanan explains Nahbi and Vophsi: one concealed God's praise of the land, the other trampled His attributes.
Numbers 13:22 is cited about the spies going up to Hebron.
Asks why the verse says and he came in the singular, when it should say and they came.
Rava teaches that Caleb separated from the spies' counsel and prayed at the graves of the forefathers in Hebron for deliverance.
Joshua did not need that because Moses already prayed for him, and Caleb changed his mind over time while Joshua opposed the spies from the start.
Explains the names Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai by their deeds, and the sons of Anak by their great height.
Asks how Hebron could have been built seven years before Zoan, since a father does not build for a younger son first.
Hebron was seven times more fruitful than Zoan and is stony, since it was used for burials, though Egypt is the finest land.
Genesis 13:10 is cited: the land was like the garden of God and like the land of Egypt.
Zoan was the finest land in Egypt, where Pharaoh's princes lived.
Isaiah 30:4 is cited: the princes were in Zoan, showing Zoan was the best land.
Even so, Hebron was seven times more fruitful than Zoan, and Hebron is stony.
Asks whether Hebron is stony, since Absalom went to Hebron to fulfil a vow, as II Samuel 15:7 says.
Rav Avya, or Rabba bar bar Hanan, explains that Absalom went to bring sheep specifically from Hebron.
A baraita is cited: rams for the altar come from Moab and sheep from Hebron, showing Hebron has rich pasture.
From the same source, Hebron is not suited to agriculture, since its thin soil yields grass that fattens livestock.
Numbers 13:25 is cited: the spies returned from searching the land at the end of forty days.

35a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Yohanan in R. Shimon ben Yohai's name: the going of the spies is compared to their coming back, both done with wicked counsel.
Numbers 13:27-28 is cited: the spies praised the land and then said the people there are strong, which raises the question of their slander.
R. Yohanan, citing R. Meir, gives a principle: slander that does not begin with a true statement does not endure to its end.
Numbers 13:30 is cited: Caleb stilled the people toward Moses.
Rabba explains stilled as persuaded; Joshua began speaking, and the people mocked him for having a severed head and no children.
Caleb feared being silenced, so he spoke about Moses, and the people thought he was disparaging Moses and fell silent.
Caleb recalled God's deeds and urged going up, but the men who went with him said they could not overcome the people, who are stronger.
R. Hanina bar Pappa reads stronger than us as stronger than Him, so the spies spoke heresy about God.
Numbers 13:32 is cited: the land consumes its inhabitants, which the spies offered as proof the land was bad.
Rava explains God intended the deaths for the spies' good so the Canaanites were preoccupied with mourning, while the spies took it as evidence against the land.
Numbers 13:33 is cited: the spies said they were like grasshoppers in their own eyes and in the eyes of the people.
Rav Mesharshiyya says the spies were liars, since they could not have known how the Canaanites saw them.
The Gemara responds: the spies hid in cedar trees and heard Canaanites call them grasshoppers, so the spies did know.
Numbers 14:1 is cited: the whole congregation lifted up their voice and wept.
R. Yohanan says that day was the eve of the Ninth of Av, when God made the weeping a gratuitous weeping for all generations, and the people sought to stone Moses and Aaron.
Numbers 14:10 is cited: the glory of the Lord appeared in the Tent of Meeting just as they sought to stone the leaders.
R. Hiyya bar Abba explains that they took stones and threw them upward as if to strike God.
Numbers 14:37 is cited: those who brought the evil report died by plague before the Lord.
R. Shimon ben Lakish explains that they died an unusual death.
R. Hanina bar Pappa, citing R. Sheila, says their tongues fell onto their navels, with worms moving between tongue and navel.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak says they died of diphtheria, a choking disease.
Once the last of Israel came up from the Jordan, the water returned to its place, as the priests stepped out of the river.
Joshua 4:18 is cited: the waters returned to their place and overflowed all banks as before, after the priests came out of the Jordan.
The Ark and its bearers were on the east side while the people were on the west, so the Ark carried its bearers across.
Joshua 4:11 is cited: when all the people were passed over, the Ark of the Lord passed on, with the priests before the people.
Uzzah was punished for not taking proper care of the Ark.
I Chronicles 13:9 is cited: at the threshing floor Uzzah put forth his hand to hold the Ark, and God says the Ark can carry itself.
II Samuel 6:7 is cited: the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzzah and God smote him there.
R. Yohanan and R. Elazar disagree: one holds Uzzah forgot that the Ark carries itself, the other that he relieved himself before it.
II Samuel 6:7 is cited: he died there with the Ark of God.
R. Yohanan says Uzzah entered the World-to-Come, since the Ark exists forever and he died with the Ark.
II Samuel 6:8 is cited: David was displeased because the Lord had broken forth upon Uzzah.
R. Elazar says vayyiḥar means David's face changed colors and darkened like baked bread from displeasure.
The Gemara objects: if vayyiḥar means that, why is it not read so when it refers to God, and the answer is that anger is written there.
Rava teaches that David was punished for calling matters of Torah songs, as Psalms 119:54 shows.
God replies that Torah demands full attention, so He caused David to err in a matter even schoolchildren know: the Ark must be carried on shoulders, not in a wagon.
I Samuel 6:19 is cited: God smote the men of Beit Shemesh because they gazed upon the Ark.
Asks why gazing upon the Ark warranted God's punishment of the men of Beit Shemesh.
R. Abbahu and R. Elazar differ: they were reaping and prostrating at once, or they also spoke denigrating words.

35b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks who angered the Ark so much that it went into captivity, and who came to appease it.
I Samuel 6:19 is cited: God smote seventy men of the people, fifty thousand men.
R. Abbahu and R. Elazar disagree: seventy men each worth fifty thousand, or fifty thousand each worth the seventy sanhedrin members.
II Samuel 6:13 and I Chronicles 15:26 are cited: David sacrificed an ox and a fatling after six steps, and seven oxen and seven rams in all.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel holds that David sacrificed an ox and fatling after every step.
Rav Hisda objects: if so, every step needed a new altar, filling Eretz Yisrael with altars.
Rav Hisda's correct reading: an ox and fatling per six steps, and seven oxen and rams per six sets of six steps.
I Chronicles 13:9 and II Samuel 6:6 are cited, the threshing floor named kidon in one and nakhon in the other.
R. Yohanan explains the Ark was like a javelin at first, causing Uzzah's death, and later it was established at Obed Edom.
The Gemara states three sets of stones: one Moses set up in Moab, citing Deuteronomy 1:5 and 27:3.
A verbal analogy between be'er and ba'er in Deuteronomy shows Moses also wrote the Torah on stones.
Joshua set up twelve stones in the Jordan and twelve in Gilgal; a baraita says Israel wrote the Torah on stones and then plastered them.
R. Shimon asks how the nations of that time could learn Torah if the writing was plastered over.
R. Yehuda replies that God gave the nations extra understanding, so they had their scribes peel off the plaster and copy it, which sealed their doom.
R. Shimon holds the Jews wrote the text on the plaster and below for the gentiles, and if the gentiles had repented they would have been accepted.
Rava bar Sheila explains R. Shimon's view from Isaiah 33:12: the nations were punished on account of matters of plaster.
Asks how R. Yehuda, who holds the Torah was not written on plaster, reads that same verse.
The gentiles are like plaster, which has no remedy but burning, so the nations have no remedy but burning in Gehenna.
Asks in accordance with whose opinion the baraita about captured Canaanites outside Eretz Yisrael is taught.
Deuteronomy 21:10 is cited, implying that captured Canaanites outside Eretz Yisrael are accepted if they repent and may live in the land.

36a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks in accordance with whose opinion the baraita about the hornet and Canaanites outside the land is taught.
It accords with R. Shimon, who holds the command to destroy the Canaanites does not apply to those outside Eretz Yisrael.
Come and see the miracles of that day: Israel crossed the Jordan and reached the mountains, and whoever stood before them was struck with terror.
Exodus 23:27 and 15:16 are cited: the terror that falls on the nations until the people pass over, marking the first arrival.
The second arrival lacked miracles only because of sin, so the people built the altar on Ebal, wrote the Torah on stones, and went on to Gilgal.
Joshua 4:3 is cited: carry the stones over and lay them down in the lodging place where you shall lodge this night.
This night means only one night, so the stones need not be placed at every lodging place.
Joshua 4:20 is cited: the twelve stones taken out of the Jordan were set up in Gilgal.
A baraita teaches that the hornet did not cross the Jordan with the Israelites.
Asks whether this is so, since Exodus 23:28 says God will send the hornet before them.
R. Shimon ben Lakish says the hornet blinded and castrated the Amorites from the Jordan, citing Amos 2:9; Rav Pappa says there were two hornets, Moses's and Joshua's.
Mishna: six tribes ascended to Mount Gerizim, as Joshua 8:33 describes the half of them in front of each mountain.
Asks what the term and the half of them means, since it seems to refer to an existing division.
Rav Kahana explains that the tribes were divided on the mountains as they were on the stones of the ephod.
The Gemara objects: the High Priest's ephod had two stones with six tribe names on each, per Exodus 28:10, so the division was not by mountain.
The stones differ in order: the second lists tribes by birth order while the first begins with Judah, and each stone bore twenty-five letters.
Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel begins to offer a further view on the stones.

36b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The names were divided on the ephod not as in Numbers 1 but as in the second book of Exodus, by the order of birth.
Explains the arrangement: Leah's sons in birth order, Rachel's sons at the ends, and the handmaids' sons in the middle, named by their father's names.
A baraita contradicts Rav Kahana's view that the ephod division matched the mountains, a conclusive refutation.
Asks what the phrase and the half of them facing Mount Ebal means.
A baraita explains that the Gerizim half was larger, because Levi stood at the bottom between the mountains.
Objects: on the contrary, Levi at the bottom would make the Ebal half smaller, so the explanation does not hold.
Replies that the descendants of Joseph were among those at the bottom, and Joseph's tribe was numerous.
Joshua 17:14-15 is cited: the children of Joseph claimed to be a great people, and Joshua told them to go up to the forest.
Joshua told them to hide in the forests so the evil eye would not harm them; Joseph's tribe replied the evil eye has no power over them, citing Genesis 49:22.
Genesis 48:16 is cited: as fish in the sea are covered by water and unaffected by the evil eye, so Joseph's descendants are protected.
Asks how the names on the ephod contain fifty letters when counting only forty-nine.
R. Yitzhak says a letter was added to Joseph's name, citing Psalms 81:6, Yehosef.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzhak objects: the names must be written according to birth, and Joseph was not called Yehosef at birth.
Benjamin is spelled in full with a second yod where he is born, citing Genesis 35:18, so his name appears with it on the ephod.
R. Shimon Hasida taught that Joseph, who sanctified God's name in private, had the letter heh added, and Judah, who did so publicly, had God's name in his.
Joseph sanctified God's name in private, as Genesis 39:11 shows; R. Yohanan and Rav and Shmuel dispute whether he entered to do his work or his desire.
Genesis 39:11 continues: no one of the men of the house was there.
Asks how so large and important a wicked man's house could be empty of people.
The school of R. Yishmael taught that it was their festival and all went to their idol house, while she, claiming sickness, stayed with Joseph.
Genesis 39:12 is cited: she caught him by his garment and said lie with me.
At that moment his father's image appeared in the window and warned Joseph that his name would be erased from the stones of the ephod.
Proverbs 29:3 and Genesis 49:24 are cited: a companion of harlots wastes riches, and his bow abode firm.
R. Yohanan in R. Meir's name explains his bow returned to strength, and the Mighty One of Jacob who etched his name on the ephod was Jacob's might.
Psalms 80:2 is cited: Shepherd of Israel who leads like the flock of Joseph.
A baraita: Joseph was deserving of twelve tribes descending from him, as Jacob had, since he was the son of Jacob.
Genesis 37:2 is cited: these are the generations of Jacob, Joseph.
Joseph did not merit this because of his emission between his fingernails, yet his brother Benjamin's ten sons were named after Joseph.
Genesis 46:21 is cited: the sons of Benjamin, Bela, Becher, Ashbel and others.
Explains each name in Benjamin's family as relating to Joseph: swallowed among nations, firstborn of Rachel, sent into captivity, pleasing, my brother and leader, wedding canopy, descended.
R. Hiyya bar Abba reports R. Yohanan: when Pharaoh made Joseph ruler, his astrologers objected to a former slave, but Pharaoh saw royal traits.
The astrologers object: if he is royal, he should know seventy languages, as royal children learn them.
Gabriel taught him the languages, but he could not learn all of them, so God added a heh to his name and he answered Pharaoh in every language.
Joseph spoke Hebrew, which Pharaoh could not learn, so Pharaoh made him swear not to reveal it.
Years later Joseph asked Pharaoh for release from his oath to bury his father, and Pharaoh let him go to bury Jacob as he was sworn.
Asks what the incident was in which Judah sanctified God's name in public.
Baraita: when Israel stood at the Red Sea, the tribes argued over who would enter first, and then Judah leapt in first.

37a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Benjamin's tribe descended into the sea first.
Psalm 68:28 read as descending into the sea, not ruling.
Judah's princes stoned Benjamin for going in first.
Psalm 68:28 about the princes of Judah and their council.
Benjamin merited hosting the Divine Presence in its territory.
Moses' blessing for Benjamin in Deuteronomy 33:12.
Rabbi Yehuda rejects Rabbi Meir's account of the incident.
Alternative account: each tribe refused to go in first.
Nahshon ben Amminadab went into the sea first.
Hosea 12:1 read as Judah descending with God.
Psalm 69 cited as the tradition explaining Nahshon's prayer.
Moses prolonged his prayer and God rebuked him.
Moses replies that he cannot do anything more.
God's command to Moses in Exodus 14:15-16.
Therefore Judah merited to rule over Israel.
Psalm 114:2 on Judah as sanctuary and Israel as dominion.
Why Judah is the sanctuary and Israel the dominion.
Because the sea saw it and fled.
Baraita introduces Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view.
Levi cannot be placed below or above, since each is already stated.
How can this be resolved?
Only the elders of priesthood and Levites stood below.
Rabbi Yoshiya: any Levite fit to serve stood below.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: all stood below and turned to bless or curse.
What is the meaning of al in Deuteronomy 27:12?
Al means adjacent, as a baraita teaches.
Leviticus 24:7 on frankincense placed on the rows.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says al means adjacent.
Does al mean adjacent or literally on?
Exodus 40:3 on screening the Ark with the curtain.
So al must mean adjacent.
Mishna: blessing and curse said facing the two mountains, with Amen.
Tosefta: general and particular blessings and curses, and the mitzva to learn and keep Torah.

37b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Counts the covenants: sixteen at each of three events, and the same pattern in the blessings.
Deuteronomy 28:69 and 29:8 show covenants at Sinai, Moab and the Tent of Meeting.
Therefore forty-eight covenants were made for each mitzva.
Rabbi Shimon removes Gerizim and Ebal and adds the Tent of Meeting in the desert.
Explains that the tanna'im disagree, as a baraita teaches.
Rabbi Yishmael: general mitzvot were given at Sinai, details at the Tent of Meeting.
Rabbi Akiva: both general and detailed mitzvot were given at Sinai, repeated in Moab.
Baraita conclusion: every mitzva has forty-eight covenants.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda: each mitzva has 603,550 covenants, one per Israelite.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: each Israelite is a guarantor for every other, so the count is multiplied.
What is the difference between the two positions?
Rav Mesharshiyya: the difference is a guarantor's guarantor.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Nachmani taught that the whole passage refers only to adulterers.
The entire passage of curses is stated only regarding adultery.
Deuteronomy 27:15 cited to support the adultery reading of the curse.
Is a curse sufficient punishment for an idol worshipper?
Rather, the curse concerns a child of forbidden relations who turned to idolatry, cursing his parents.
Baraita cites Deuteronomy 11:29 on giving the blessing on Gerizim and the curse on Ebal.
Why does the verse need to state this, since the location is already known?
Deuteronomy 27:12-13 is cited: the tribes stand on Gerizim and Ebal for blessing and curse.
Rather, the verse teaches that the blessing must precede the curse.
Might all blessings precede all curses?
The singular blessing and curse in the verse show otherwise.
One blessing precedes each curse, but not all blessings precede all curses.
Analogies (hekesh) between blessing and curse: Levites, loud voice, Hebrew, general and specific.
Just as the curse gets Amen from both groups, so does the blessing.
Mishna: the priestly blessing is recited differently in the country and in the Temple.

38a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Priests lift their hands in the Temple, except the High Priest, who keeps them below the frontplate.
Rabbi Yehuda: even the High Priest lifts his hands above the frontplate.
Leviticus 9:22 shows Aaron lifting his hands to bless the people.
The Sages taught a baraita on the wording of the Priestly Benediction in Numbers 6:23.
Must the Priestly Benediction be recited in the sacred tongue, or in any language?
Verbal analogy with Deuteronomy 27:12 shows it must be recited in Hebrew.
Rabbi Yehuda: no analogy needed, since the word thus shows the exact wording is required.
Another baraita on the same verse.
Must the blessing be recited standing, or even sitting?
Verbal analogy with Deuteronomy 27:12 shows it is recited standing.
Rabbi Natan: no analogy needed, since the verse itself requires standing.
Deuteronomy 10:8 is cited for the inference.
Just as service is performed standing, so the blessing is recited standing.
From where do we know that the service itself is performed standing?
Deuteronomy 18:5 teaches that service is performed standing.
Another baraita on the wording of the verse.
Must the blessing be recited with raised hands, or without?
Verbal analogy with Leviticus 9:22 shows the blessing is recited with raised hands.
Rabbi Yonatan objects: the analogy should also limit the blessing to the High Priest, the New Moon and communal service.
Rabbi Natan replies that the analogy is unnecessary since the verse itself teaches this.
Deuteronomy 18:5 links his sons to him and forever, and ties the blessing to service.
Another baraita on the wording of the verse.
Must the blessing use the ineffable name, or only the substitute name?
Numbers 6:27 says they shall put My name, meaning the unique name.
Might one think the ineffable name applies even outside the Temple?
Verbal analogy with Deuteronomy 12:5 limits the name to the Temple.
Rabbi Yoshiya: this can be derived from a verse without analogy.
Exodus 20:21 is cited: wherever I cause My name to be mentioned, I will come to you.
The verse must be read by transposition: the name is mentioned only in the Temple.
Another baraita on the wording of the verse.
From where do we derive that converts, women and freed slaves are included?
The verse says say to them, meaning to all the Jewish people.
Another baraita on the face-to-face wording.
Must the blessing be face to face, or only facing the back of the necks?
The verse says say to them, like a person speaking to another.
Another baraita on the audibility of the blessing.
Must the blessing be recited aloud, or only in a whisper?
The verse says say to them, like a person speaking to another, so it is aloud.
Abaye: with two priests the leader calls Priests, but with one he does not call Priest.
The plural say to them shows the call requires at least two priests.
Rav Hisda: a priest calls Priests, but an Israelite does not call Priests.
The verse says say to them, a call of the priests that only a priest may make.

38b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The halakha follows Abaye, not Rav Hisda, on calling the priests.
Mnemonic listing the statements of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in this section.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi introduces his teaching on God desiring the Priestly Benediction.
From where do we know that God desires the priests' blessing?
Numbers 6:27 shows God waits for the priests to bless before He blesses.
Any priest who blesses is blessed, and one who does not bless is not blessed.
Genesis 12:3 cited: I will bless those who bless you.
A priest who does not go up to bless violates three positive mitzvot.
The three verses of the blessing are cited for the three mitzvot.
Rav: one must suspect a non-ascending priest is disqualified from the priesthood.
The two statements are not in conflict: one ascends periodically, the other never ascends.
A priest who does not ascend during the Temple service blessing may never ascend again.
Leviticus 9:22 shows the blessing is recited during the service, as with Aaron.
Is that so? Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi did ascend after the service blessing.
They began walking to the platform during the blessing and arrived only after it ended.
Baraita of Rabbi Oshaya: only a priest who never began walking is excluded.
Mishna: a priest who is certain he can raise his hands may recite the blessing.
If he never began to walk, how is he permitted to bless?
He moved slightly to show he wished to ascend, and so the same applies.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: the cup of blessing is given only to a generous person.
Proverbs 22:9 read as he who has a good eye will bless, not will be blessed.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi introduces his teaching on birds recognizing miserly people.
From where do we learn that even birds recognize miserly people?
Proverbs 1:17 says the net is spread in vain before every winged bird.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: whoever benefits from a miser transgresses a prohibition.
Proverbs 23:6-7 cited: do not eat the bread of one with an evil eye.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: one transgresses two prohibitions.
Proverbs 23:6 cited: do not eat and do not desire.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: the broken-neck heifer is brought only because of miserly people.
Deuteronomy 21:7 cited: our hands have not shed this blood.
Did it enter our hearts that the court elders are murderers?
Rather, they declare they did not dismiss him without food or escort, faulting miserly people.
Adda, citing Rabbi Simlai: in an all-priest synagogue, all of them ascend to bless.
For whom do they then bless?
Rabbi Zeira: they bless their brethren who are in the fields.
Is that so? A baraita taught that those standing behind priests are excluded.
Abba, son of Rav Minyamin bar Chiya, taught that those behind priests are excluded.
The cases differ: when compelled to be away they are included, otherwise not.
Rav Shimi of Birte deShichorei taught that some priests ascend and others answer amen.
If ten priests remain to answer amen, only some ascend; otherwise all ascend.
The Gemara returns to Abba's teaching that those behind priests are not included.
Does a partition interpose, unlike a tall person or a chest?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: even an iron partition does not separate Israel from its Father.
What is the halakha for people standing to the sides of the priests?
Abba Mar cites a mishna on sprinkling for impurity to resolve the side question.

39a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Sprinkling toward one's sides is valid, since the sides count as in front of him.
Rava bar Rav Huna: once a Torah scroll is opened, conversation is prohibited, even about halakha.
Nehemiah 8:5 cited: standing before the open book means silence.
Job 32:16 cited to show that standing means not speaking.
Rabbi Zeira, citing Rav Hisda, states the source of the prohibition.
Nehemiah 8:3 cited: the people listened to the book of the law.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: a priest who did not wash his hands may not lift them to bless.

Explanation of how the ritual of the heifer is ordered, citing the verse

Proof verses from Proverbs and Deuteronomy that the king and the High Priest judge
Does Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov dispute only about the king and High Priest, or also about the Sanhedrin
Rav Yosef brings a baraita with Deuteronomy 17:8 showing that the place itself causes the judges to come out
How many judges should go out, and for what purpose, if the matter is elective
Song of Songs cites a round goblet with twenty-three judges, showing the Sanhedrin of twenty-three is the count

Shall we say the mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda and not the Rabbis

Yes, that is so

The Rabbis derive forgotten standing grain from the words when you reap your harvest in your field
Rabbi Yehuda needs the word for the teaching of Rabbi Abbahu

Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda follows Rabbi Yehuda's view

Baraita: a corpse is one not strangled, not writhing on the ground, not buried in a heap, hanging, or floating
Rabbi Elazar says in all these cases they break the heifer's neck if there is a corpse
Rabbi Yosei ben Yehuda objects: Rabbi Elazar must agree a strangled body in a dunghill does not count
Rabbi Elazar replies that the word slain is written in an extra sense

Why does the mishna state that measuring is only to a city with a court, which seems obvious

Mishna: if the corpse is between two towns, each brings a heifer, and Jerusalem does not bring one, per Rabbi Eliezer
Mishna: if the head and body are in different places, one brings the head near the body, per Rabbi Eliezer
Rabbi Akiva holds the body is brought near the head
Mishna: the disputed clauses on the point from which measuring begins, navel, nose, or the place of the wound
What is the reason for Rabbi Eliezer's view
It is possible to measure precisely when the corpse is near, and Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes
What do the two positions dispute, given the later clause about where measuring starts
Rabbi Yitzchak: the dispute concerns a corpse of mitzva, which gets its own place for burial
Restatement of the dispute: head and body placed in different places, and which is brought to which
In what do they dispute
One view holds the body stays in place and the head falls; the other holds the head is where the body falls
Psalms and Jeremiah are cited for the embryo being formed from the head or from the navel

Genesis 7:22 proves that all agree life is in the nostrils

Mishna: the elders of Jerusalem release themselves and the heifer is taken to a rough valley and its neck is broken

A kal vachomer argument: if two blemishes disqualify a heifer, a blemish should disqualify it, limited by the verse
Rav's ruling: a heifer on which the rope of sacks was placed is disqualified
Verses from Numbers and Deuteronomy derive that other labors disqualify the heifer as the yoke does
The verse is needed to exclude sacrifices, which are not disqualified by labor
A proposed kal vachomer from the heifer to sacrifices, that labor should disqualify them too
The argument can be refuted, since the verse is needed for those sacrifices that labor does disqualify
The rule is derived from one verse and also from another verse
Leviticus 22:22 is cited: do not offer these to the Lord, so you may not offer blemished sacrifices
You may not offer these, but you may offer sacrifices in which service was done
The verse is needed to limit the rule to permitted service, not forbidden service, and the rule derives from the same verse
Leviticus 22:25 is cited: no foreigner may offer the bread of your God from any of these
You may not offer these, but you may offer sacrifices in which service was done
The verse is needed for the case where the service was done on the sacrifices as sacrifices, not as ordinary animals
Rav Yehuda cites Rav: a heifer with a rope of sacks placed on it is disqualified, until it pulls
A baraita objects: the verse only shows labor disqualifies, so the kal vachomer should apply to other labors
A gezera shava: the word yoke in both verses means other labors disqualify as in the heifer case
What is the refutation of the kal vachomer, and what would be the counter argument
The sacrifices themselves could prove the point, and the gezera shava is restated: until it pulls
It is a tannaitic dispute: some derive the rule from the heifer, others from the verse on the heifer's body
Baraita: from Numbers 19:2 the verse excludes other labors not performed on the yoke
Objection: the verse may be an exclusion of a general rule, so only what is specified is included
A parallel baraita on the heifer: the verse teaches that a yoke disqualifies both during and outside service
Objection: the verse is a general and specific pair, so only the specified case is included, and the rule is limited
Rabbi Abbahu asks Rabbi Yochanan how much pulling makes a yoke
Rabbi Yochanan answers: as much as the full yoke
They wonder whether the measure is lengthwise or widthwise
Rabbi Yochanan explains the width is a handbreadth, which matters for buying and selling
Rabbi Yochanan ben Shaul: the Torah has the heifer brought to a valley so that the one who did not let him produce fruit is atoned
What is meant by fruit: procreation, and if so, what of the old man and the eunuch
The heifer's neck is broken only for a mitzva, and the rough valley is taken as meant literally
The Sages taught from where it is known that the word eitan means hard

Baraita on Deuteronomy 21:4: Rabbi Yoshiyah and Rabbi Yonatan dispute whether the prohibition is about the past or the future

Rabbi Yonatan reads the word which as an expansion, so plowing and other labors are included, and dragging stone is permitted
Baraita: the verse excludes labors other than plowing, derived from the phrase from any place
If so, why is the word plow written; it teaches that only work in the body of the ground is excluded
Objection: the verse may be a general and specific pair, so only what is specified is included
The elders of the city wash their hands, as the mishna states
Baraita: Deuteronomy 21:6 is read to show the washing takes place at the site of the heifer's neck-breaking
Text of the declaration: our hands did not shed this blood, our eyes did not see it, and the court did not shed blood
Baraita: Rabbi Meir says one is compelled to escort, and the wages of escorting have no set amount
Judges 1:24-26 is recounted: the men of Luz showed the entrance, and the man who was spared built the city named Luz
Baraita: Luz is where the blue dye is made, and the angel of death may not pass through it except for elders who have finished
Kal vachomer: if a Canaanite who neither spoke nor walked was rewarded, one who escorts on foot is rewarded more
By what did Hezekiah show them the way
Hezekiah spoke, and Rabbi Yochanan says he showed them with his finger
A baraita agrees with Rabbi Yochanan: by pointing with his finger he gained rescue for himself and his descendants
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: one who walks without an escort should study Torah, as Proverbs states
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: Pharaoh escorted Abraham four paces, which is why Pharaoh's escort is cited
Genesis 15:13 is cited: the descendants were enslaved and afflicted four hundred years
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: one who lends to his fellow within four cubits of the town is not harmed
Ravina escorted Rava bar Yitzchak, and when they reached four cubits within the town, the harm came and he was saved
Baraita: a teacher escorts a student to the town boundary; Rav Sheshet adds a parsa, or three parsa for a master who is not a teacher of record

Rav Mordechai escorted Rav Ashi from Hagronia to the bridge of Kipi, or the bridge of Dura

Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel: wherever the Sages cast their eyes, death or poverty follows
Shmuel: he saw that all of them were conceived on Yom Kippur
Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha: he saw their hair locks, as with the Amorites
Rabbi Yochanan: he saw that there was no moisture of a mitzva in them

Deuteronomy 15:9 is cited: beware lest there be a wicked thought in your heart against the needy

What are the stirrers

Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar on what was lost after the Temple's destruction, while the Sages say immorality and sorcery consumed everything
How do we know that the Sanhedrin's ceasing is written

Rav: the ear that heard the song is uprooted; Rava: song in the house, destruction in the threshold
Zephaniah 2:14 is cited: the voice sings in the window, desolation is at the threshold
What is meant by the cedar's beams in the verse
Rabbi Yitzchak: it refers to a house enclosed by cedars, which is still a city, so even a house enclosed by cedars is shaken
Rav Ashi: learn from this that destruction begins at the threshold, and one can also learn it from another verse
Isaiah 24:12 is cited: desolation remains at the gate
Mar bar Rav Ashi remarks: the verse was clear to me when the ox gores
Rav Huna banned song of the flutes and the musician, and the story of the prices of geese and wheat, and Rav Chisda's loss
Rav Yosef: men who sing with women and women who sing with men cause lewdness, like fire in straw
What practical difference is there between these cases, to nullify or to forbid
Rabbi Yochanan: anyone who drinks to four kinds of music brings five punishments on the world
Isaiah 5:11-12 is cited: woe to those who rise early to pursue strong drink, with harp and lyre, and do not regard the work of the Lord
What is written after this

Exile is caused by lack of knowledge, famine by hunger and thirst for the Torah, which is forgotten by its learners

Lowliness causes insult to the Holy One, blessed be He, and the lowliness of Israel is caused by it

The faithful men ceased
Rabbi Yitzchak: these are the people who do not believe in the Holy One, blessed be He
Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer the Great says anyone who has bread in his basket and asks what he will eat tomorrow is of little faith, as Rabbi Elazar also says
What is meant by the verse who despised the day of small things, and what caused the righteous to be despised
The smallness of faith caused the righteous to be despised, because they did not believe in the Holy One
Rava says these are the small children of the wicked of Israel

ranges.en: The children of the righteous who were corrupted say before God that He will punish them in the future, so why did their fathers' teeth become dull
Rabbi Ila'a bar Yevarechya: were it not for David's prayer, all Israel would be sellers of myriads of ... and the verse is cited
Psalm 9:21 is cited: set fear upon them, O Lord, that the nations may know they are only men
Were it not for Habakkuk's prayer, two Torah scholars would have covered themselves with one cloak and studied together
Habakkuk 3:2 is cited: O Lord, I have heard your report; in the midst of the years make it known
Two Torah scholars walking on the road with no words of Torah between them deserve to be burned by fire
2 Kings 2:11 is cited: as they went on talking, a chariot of fire appeared and separated them
The explanation: when there is conversation the punishment does not apply, but without it they deserve to be burned
Two Torah scholars living in one city who are not comfortable with each other in law, one dies and one goes into exile
Deuteronomy 4:42 and Hosea 4:6 are cited: the murderer flees to the city, and the people are destroyed for lack of knowledge
Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiya: any Torah scholar who studies under hardship has his prayer heard
Isaiah 30:19 is cited: he will surely be gracious to you at the sound of your cry
Isaiah 30:20 is cited: the Lord will give you bread of adversity and water of affliction
Rabbi Abbahu: they adjure such a person by the radiance of the Shekhinah
Isaiah 30:20 is cited: your eyes shall see your teacher
Rabbi Achah bar Chanina: the veil is not closed before the teacher
Isaiah 30:20 is cited: your teacher will not be hidden any more
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, citing Rabbi Yehoshua: since the Temple was destroyed, the curse prevails
Rava: each day the curse of one is greater than the other's
Deuteronomy 28:67 is cited: in the morning you shall say, would it were evening, and in the evening, would it were morning
What is meant by morning, is it tomorrow's morning, which no one knows
Rather, it refers to the passing day; and why does the world endure, through the holiness of the order, Rava's aggadic name
Job 10:22 is cited: a land of darkness and deep shadow with no order
Objection: but there are orders, and the verse says light shines from darkness, so the dew and the taste of fruit can return
Baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says purity cancels the taste and smell of tithe, and tithe cancels the fat of grain
Anecdotes: Rav Huna found a bundle of dates, and his son Rabbah tasted it; Rav Achah bar Yaakov and the son of Rav Yaakov's daughter; and the proverb that a father's mercy is for the children

Mishna: in the war of Vespasian they decreed against wreaths for bridegrooms and the bridal chamber; in the war of Titus against teaching Greek; the bride may go out in a litter, though the rabbis permitted it

When Rabbi Meir died the parable-makers ceased; when Ben Azzai died the diligent ceased; when Ben Zoma died the expounders ceased; when Rabbi Akiva died honor of the Torah ceased; and the pious ceased when Rabbi Yosei Ketanta died
Why was he called Ketanta

When Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai died the glory of wisdom ceased; when Rabban Gamliel died honor ceased; then purity and separation, Rabbi Yishmael's glory of priesthood, and Rabbi's humility and fear of sin
The Gemara introduces a baraita of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair
Baraita: since the Temple was destroyed, friends and free men were ashamed, the men of deeds were weakened, and the strong and the slanderers prevailed
Rabbi Eliezer the Great: since the Temple was destroyed, the sages became like scribes, scribes like attendants, and attendants like the common people

Rav, Shmuel and Levi dispute which oils or myrtle and reed products are permitted or forbidden
What is the irus mentioned in the mishna
Rabbi Elazar: irus is a drum with one head; Rabbah bar Rav Huna made a drum for his son, and his father told him to make it from a one-mouthed jug
Mishna: in the war of Titus they decreed against the crowns of brides
What are the crowns of brides
Rabbi Yochanan: a city of gold, so the crown is a city of gold, while the Sages allow a diadem of myrtle
Baraita: the crown is a city of gold, but one makes it like a cap of gold; they also decreed against the canopy of bridegrooms
What is the canopy of bridegrooms
The baraita explains: these are the golden crimson canopies, but one may make a silk canopy and hang on it whatever one wishes
Baraita: one should not teach his son Greek

Baraita: when the Hasmonean kings besieged each other, Hyrcanus was outside and Aristobulus inside; a Greek-wise elder revealed that the sacrifices were being sent a pig; and the story of the land of Israel and the stones of Ma'aleh
Is that so? For the Master said Sorsi language in Israel, and Rav Yosef said Aramaic in Babylon; so is Greek wisdom forbidden
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel citing Rabban Shimon from Lamentations 3:51: my eyes grieve for the daughters of my city
My father had a thousand children, five hundred learned Torah and five hundred learned Greek wisdom; only I and my uncle's son were left, while Rabban Gamliel's house was close to the kingdom
Baraita: one may teach Greek wisdom to those close to the kingdom, and in the last war they decreed that a bride not go out in a litter
The reason is modesty

When Rabban Yochanan died wisdom ceased; when Rabbi Eliezer died the Torah scroll was hidden; when Rabbi Akiva died the arms of the Torah ceased; when Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah died the crowns of wisdom ceased
Proverbs 14:24 is cited: the crown of the wise is their riches
When Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa died the men of deeds ceased; when Abba Yosei ben Ketonta died the pious ceased
Why was Abba Yosei ben Ketonta called that name
Because he was the smallest of the pious
When Ben Azzai died the diligent ceased; when Ben Zoma died the expounders ceased; when Rabban Shimon died the swarms of troubles increased; when Rabbi died humility and fear of sin ceased
Rav Yosef tells the Tanna not to teach humility since it exists, and Rav Nachman says not to teach fear of sin; closing of Tractate Sotah
